item.description:
Sorry! Rare lapse yesterday, and I forgot to update the redirect. Many of you know the Secret Code, and can adjust the URL, but if not, yesterday's big Bleat is
here
.
It's a vacation week,
not a Hiatus week. That means diminished above-the-fold, and rejiggered below-the-fold. I've decided to put Main Street on Wednesday, because I have an excess of completed Main Streets and a surfeit of Clippings.
We'll skip ahead a week to the inevitable:
Yes, commish, you've done it. He's going to
your daughter's house.
It's not as if it's changed him, or installed something that wasn't there. The potion released him.
Will the Spirit get married? Come back tomorrow to find out.
Welcome to Tripp. Probably the sister city of Zap. Itâs a wonder the hippies didnât go there.
Itâs the police station.
It has three reviews, one of which is a solitary star. You can probably guess why.
The sign says âIdle Hours,â indicating a bar, but it doesnât seem to be going today.
The sign says itâs for sale. The other signs indicate it was a restaurant / beer garden. The 2008 version has an Italian flag, indicating pizza and spaghetti.
Good luck to whomeverâs next.
Previous view: pizza joint.
View before that: BOWL.
An old bank, still a bank. You wonder . . .
Was the floor elevated for some reason?
The side:
It's an odd selection of windows for the back of the building, a side street location. It must have been custom-made for an important client.
Itâs just so sad. Thatâs all. The Tripp State Bank. Cornice ground off, windows boarded and painbted long ago.
Sure, the old windows probably made the place more expensive to heat and cool, but . . .
Well, no, you can't expect them to carry the weight just for civic beauty.
Still a pity.
Iâm starting to regret this visit.
It's an odd selection of windows for the back of the building, a side street location. It must have been custom-made for an important client.
Still a going concern, but they seemed to have closed up the front office a long time ago.
If I had to say, I'd bet it was a grocery store.
And I'd guess it moved.
That wasn't built as a grocery store, of course. At least the bricked-up windows don't look too bad.
They just kept adding things. And we all know what the oldest part used to be, don't we?
And here we end.
That'll do! I may be short-shrifting this week, but there are Motels, and the Substack's up. Thank you for your indulgence.

item.description:
As is the way of things,
I stopped at Central Nervous System dispensaron Friday afternoon to pick up this and that and enjoy the samples. So many! Iâd started with a sip of a Woolcott bourbon and cream, and had told the demonstrator âyou know, this is candy for people who canât hold their whiskeyâ and she couldnât argue. She asked if I wanted to try the other one and I said Alas, I have diabetes now, and we smiled and I moved on. There was a nice suburban mom handing out samples of a particular winery, whites and reds, four bottles total; I had two. You just canât be greedy. I was honest with my opinion:
eh.
I moved along to the next demonstration station, also run by another nice suburban mom, whose kids were no doubt grown and out but came back for the holidays, and she lived in a nice house with her husband who was still working but looking at retiring, and they didnât know if theyâd stay or move, she really didnât want to think about it, you know? She did this on Fridays for pin money and just, you know, be out there! We had a long talk about the cabernet, which was the busiest wine Iâve had in a long time. We both agreed that the nine-dollar chardonnay was a keeper, and I said it would go well with anything and she said it didnât have to go with anything at all, as far as she was concerned.
While I was looking at the gins - noting, with satisfaction, one of the gins whose campaign Daughter worked on - the short clerk with the enormous timpani belly and untucked shirt hove into view and started challenging my gin choices. Thereâs always an undercurrent of subtle menace with this guy, an unspoken quantity of VAST KNOWLEDGE of which you can take advantage, or not, your call, your loss. I chose a gin he said was the oldest in London, and I wanted to say âso it was afflicting syphilis-suffering aged-out prostitutes in Hogarthian alleyways, you mean?â
Cheerful suburban mom at the checkout, bright how-ya-doinâ mood, and as with all the other cheerful suburban moms at the place, itâs realize Iâve been sorta kinda flirting with all of them? In a way? Thereâs a certain conversational groove that turns from rote product demonstration into conspiratorial banter. I like to make them all laugh, although of course theyâre paid to flatter the customers, and I think: getting tiny samples of cabernet in plastic cups at 4 PM on a Friday is now my version of a lap dance.
We were coming back from the afternoon excursion. I had been at the gym, which was mostly deserted except for a big conspicuous grunter who was working with bands. I can understand the occasional URGH when hoisting plates, but bands? Iâm 5â4â and 68 over here and Iâm working the 30s on bicep curls, which is my limit, and aside from one gust of effort when I pick them up, I try to keep quiet about all this. Anyway, the guyâs grunting, and then drops his bands like heâs just bench-pressed a VW Bug and saunters off with this oh yeah I rule attitude. Weâre all very impressed here at the Edina Planet Fitness, population 17.
I left, said goodbye to the front staff, and got Birch out of the car. I beep the unlock button en route, and itâs always good to see him pop up and look to see if Iâm coming.
When he got out of the car he picked up a stick heâd dropped the previous day, and carried it a while along the parking lot until he had this thought, perhaps: there will be better sticks beyond. He dropped it. We walked. I know I keep saying it, but it really was the last warm day at the lake.
It was November 20th, and it was
65 degrees.
At the watering spot there were no chairs. Some people had moved them up on the path. I dragged one back. He sat on the sand and I sat in the chair and we enjoyed the last warm day weâd have together in the year of our Lord 2026. Forecasts said 40s from here on. Forecasts said the cold was coming back, as it must. As it should. Itâs late November. The coming cold will be all the worse for this.
I wondered what I would be doing if I was back home. Sitting outside in the gazebo, maybe tossing a stick or fighting for a stick. Birch would do about three tosses before he lost focus. When we walk back from the lake he always finds an immense stick from the pile the Edina park people have heaped, and he selects one with great care, usually something of ludicrous length. Imagine a dog carrying the stick a highwire artist would use. I have to stop and break it down for him, and then he wants to fight me for it, and the leash gets tangled around leg and stick, and weâre staggering around like comic drunks. So yes, if I was at home, which doesnât exist anymore, a toss or two. Looking up to see the straggler geese heading out. Thinking about supper. It being Friday, wondering if it was time to bring up the 5 oâclock wine and cheese.
Ah well.
Back to Fred Base One for a snack and a nap. One last - surely the last - espresso on the balcony with a lease violation, before settling in to work. After supper, after dark, it was still 62, so we walked the whole circuit. The field is different now. Lights glint off new ponds.
Earlier that day Iâd seen a worker doing some things by the Slough of Despond, and I congratulated him on the work, how theyâd absolutely planed the place flat in no time. They were almost done, he said, and would knock off when the snow came. We talked about the culverts theyâd put in.
Earlier that morning Iâd seen workman struggling with a culvert issue, no idea what, and one said âhold on, let me get the hammer,â and he got hammer and pounded something on the inside of the culvert, and they all whooped with success. The world depends on guys who say âhold on let me try to hit it with a hammerâ and it turns out to work.
As much as I look forward to seeing what the park will be like in the spring, itâs strange how the space across which we rambled in the summer night is gone. The little hills are gone. The extravagant weeds and thick grass and goldenrod and thistles, all gone. All the bushes where the wee beasties lived and the rabbits hid, gone. Most of the trees, gone. What had been an array of boundless aromas for Birch is now dirt and gasoline.
We made the usual turn and went past the playground. Empty, of course. The apartment buildings were half-dark, possibly because a few units havenât been rented. They were A-class once and theyâre B minus now. If that. They used to be rented by guys who were working in the adjacent computer-industry offices that lined 77th and, of course, Computer Avenue. Guys who wore short-sleeve shirts with wide ties and pocket protectors.
Ah: a rare evening poop, solid as an Arctic core sample. Good. That takes the pressure off tomorrow morn. Iâll be able to make a full proper breakfast and take my time. Iâve good sausage, fresh hash browns, some red-pepper cheese for the eggs, and an apple pastry I can bake for the weekend sweetness. Thatâs something to look forward to.
Back to the Fred. Sit out on a lamppost base and have a lease violation. I got smilingly chided for that today by one of the young ladies who manage the property. I apologized and said I thought the wind would take away the evidence of my sins. I was at the absolute perimeter of the property, but rules are rules.
Iâd left the bottles in the car for later, and brought them up after the evening walk. I gave Birch all his medications, including the ones I had to hide in peanut butter, and set to work. We had one last walk outside before bed, and I used the new leash. The old one suffered some structural failure. The new one is retractable. He can wander away a lot farther. I noticed that he noticed, and he would stop, and look to me to see if I was still there, if we were still connected.
At the end of the night I had an Old Fashioned, and then an Isle of Skye, the official whisky of Fred Base One. I intend to inaugurate the Last House with the Isle of Skye cigar edition. An indulgence. Then I sat down to watch
Mobland
, because it was Friday. And a good one! I had not only filed two pieces, I ripped up one at 12:15 an hour before deadline and written something completely new. Gun to the head, 700 words. Iâd done a good podcast and been pleased with my ad reads and general show management. Iâd designed some new art for the 2027 Bleat, and exhausted my AI credits designing a new Bleat index redirect animation with Reddy.
A good solid day. Talked with friends on the Zoom, but didnât see a single person I knew. Itâs midnight now, freshly struck, and thereâs nothing Iâd like better than a hug and a kiss to end the day, but that part of life is over. Itâs really for the best if you donât miss it anymore, and itâs possible, some day, some night, you wonât.
Continuing
with the Spirit, from 1944: I've snipped out a lot abnout Sneezer's invention he though would stop crime. It's an inhibition lifter. One sip, and your guard comes down completely.
Not sure how that would
reduce
crime. Anyway:
Of all the people who could act without inhibitions, it's the Spirit, you'd think - he's legally dead, and lives outside the law. As you can tell, though, Ellen has plans.
Inking mistake here; the guy's suit shouldn't be dark. Anyway, you get the idea:
yoink.
In keeping with our Monday tradition, which became a "tradition" for reasons I can't recall and probably don't matter, we continue with our Monday trademark. For this year we'll do 1936.
Not the word I'd use for a child's chair.
Somehow I knew this would be underwhelming. I never liked this radio show too much. Heresy, I know.
Itâs a programmer, and it absolutely does not have to be called
Inner Sanctum.
Thatâs the radio show with the mysterious, gruesome, often supernatural aspect. It had the famous creaking door, and Raymond, the sardonic announcer given to gruesome puns. EC would make a mint off him when they stole his bit for their comic-book mascots.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
I shouldâve cleaned
the air frier today. I shouldâve taken out the Bartenderâs Friend, then thought âwhy - WHY did I buy the liquid version? What was I thinking? How can it possibly have the same abrasive power?â And then I would remember I did buy the granulated version, and set to work getting rid of the surprising remainders baked into the grill by a âsavory campfireâ pork chop. Target, 2 fr $5, and quite delicious with potatoes and a nice spinach-and-arugula salad. I shouldâve done all that, but it was 55 degrees today, and out into the world I went. Thereâll be time when the snow falls. Iâve set aside first hard snow day for some detailed cleaning.
Looking forward to seasonal dressing, but I wonder how itâll affect the daily walk down to Centennial. I donât know if the lower paths will be open. I was down there today with Birch, of course, and he went to his spot to get a drink, and there was a different fellow sitting alone in a chair staring at the water, and we chatted a bit. I almost said âdivorced?â because it seems as if the spot draws the recently abandoned.
No doubt you've met George. What a nice fellow.
He has the ability to put price tags on everything just by turning around.
His shop occasionally teleports, but he's probably used to it.
You're probably thinking "gosh, he seems like a nice old man - but he's closing his store! That's sad! I wish I could buy one of his handmade hats to salute his dedication to making the simple things in life a matter of quality and tradition."
Of course you think this, because you're still kicking yourself for not getting one of Hudson's caps:
That's a screen shot from a while ago. Probably sold out by now! Well, last I checked, this fellow - who was also an old craftsman hanging it up at the end of a long and honorable career -
was still selling knives.
Of course, it's all a lie. It makes me wonder why they're allowed to get away with it. You can't say it's like TV commercials, where you have actors pretending to be advocates for a particular product, because the assumption of artifice and theater is built into the medium. This is different, and makes you realize that A) FAKE is now the default assumption, and B) people probably yearn for something that is authentically false, that is, obviously a manufactured set-up like ads of yore.
This fellow has done a brilliant job
making fun of it.
Remember: every person who is retiring and trying to sell you something
is a scam.
Also, please sign up for my Substack!
That's about it for the week. Up and down. Not a lot more to show you, unless I left some things in the Misc folder I'd intended to expand upon . . . ah.
This was part of a round-up of new St. Paul schools in 1931, taken from that photo section I mentioned the other day. The source of the H. G. Wells picture. Remember? Anyway, I had to see if it still existed.
It looks as if it was tried and convicted and sent to School Prison.
For some reason there's a folder named Dinkytown. I don't know why I did this, but here:
Used to be a Best Steak house. See that little thing on the right with a slanted roof? No-Prize for the first person to identify its name and purpose.
Anyway:
Kitty-whumpus on the same artery: the famous Lurking McDonald's.
It was built by a railroad trench. You went down the stairs to the counter and dining room, and if you wanted some privacy you went up to the second level to look out at street level.
This was the original building:
I wish I'd seen that. It must have been beautiful at night.
And now:
So many more places to live, but not as safe. And not as interesting. I hate to be that guy, but it's true. Dinkytown was better in my day. Uptown was better when I lived there. Downtown was bustling and beautiful when I first started working there.
These things really aren't in dispute.
Back to the Spirit.
We'll conclude this story next week. If you'll recall, a sad-sack "inventor" was bothering Dolan about a crime-solving invention.
Eisner wasn't drawing the dailies. He was still in the service. The strips were handled by Lou Fine (pencils) and inked by the great & tragic Jack Cole.
Nice
Distant City
in panel 2.
You cannot guess where this is going. We'll find out next week.
I found out I had to move the next day. I did not want to go. When I said I did not want to leave my home a giant robot that looked like the one from a Queen album cover showed up and dragged me out, and I complained that I didn't even like Queen that much and didn't like the illustration on the album.
We all loved his comeback story, and he had some great new tunes.

item.description:
REINOW
THAT WAS IT
REINOW HALL
Sorry, I was talking to a guy in the elevator who was wearing an IOWA sweatshirt. Asked if he was a Hawkeye, he was, had gone to the U of I, I said I'd spent time there in a dorm - and I couldn't remember it. I said it started with R. He was no help. In fact he had a beatific expression of disengagement the whole ride up, and I think he may have blazed in the car or back in the field.
Anyway, why Reinow? We'll get to that. But first I must warn you: music bleat.
Click here to skip
to angry remarks about my city.
Warning, though: tiresome personal stuff.
Click here
to start the End of the Spirit.
The music at the gym today
was slightly less annoying but no less repetitive. If I could narrow it down: it was a minor key piece whose primary melodic component was a two-note bass line that went up one octave, and then - get this - down an octave. Having turned our heads around with that innovation, it repeated the idea while an aggravated man recited some grievances, some of which had to do with women and rivals, but not money. Of that he had plenty, we were assured.
I mentioned a song the other day that gave me a headache. Here it is. Feel free to dip in and out anywhere you want.
Of course I understand that this is not for me, an oldish fellow, <tomholland_emphasis> but </tomholland_emphasis> I listen and enjoy many things made by people forty-five years my junior. I find this ugly and unimaginative, part of the meritricious and anti-beauty Era of Insidious Teal.
Itâs not as if Iâm opposed to repetitive music. I listen to a lot of modern tunes that
donât even bother to modulate or contain singing, but are nevertheless bangers
- the linked song has crazy sloppy energy I love. You can tell it fits a specific genre of pop that flames out fast, because you go through the predictable stages:
First hearing, instant love for some reason
Second hearing, next day, you are walking around the house nodding your head
Third hearing while driving, this is perfect
Fourth hearing with a friend, you're a bit used to it
Fifth hearing, I'll probably connect this song with these times and this place
Then it slips out of the rotation, and you probably hear it a year later and recapture 74.3% of the third-hearing emotions.
Or thereâs these geezers:
It has moods and intrigue. It brings back that initial dissonant motif with a bit more tinkly gentility before it turns into a horn solo piece for a while, because why not? It evolves, moves, calls back, adds more layers. It's a conversation, not a harangue.
I remember talking with a fellow late-night radio talk show comrade at KSTP about classical music. He couldnât understand why I thought it was better than the Beatles. And I like the Beatles just fine. He granted that it was longer and more complex, but why did that make it
better?
Good question. Answer: because âbetterâ in this sense means âadditional and ever-deepening aesthetic rewards that arise from understanding the complexity, the sophistication of the composition, and the aptitude required to reproduce it." It's the difference between chess and Hangman.
Again, those donât always mean something is better. Hereâs an Elvis Costello song Iâve been singing to myself for a while, and itâs got it all. Harmonies, key changes, tempo changes, great drum fills, echoey guitars. Itâs all kinds of interesting. But itâs not as good as âHelp.â
One of the amusing things Iâve learned by watching old Elvis Costello videos - and he made a lot - is how there was absolutely no way he would ever be cool. He was an energetic and fairly anger stage performer, but heâs such a dork in the videos. I think it was David Lee Roth who said critics loved Elvis because they looked as dorky as he did.
Did I see this live on TV, as it happened? I did. He was doing a song about British fascism and thought, screw that.
EC and the Attractions were on the show because Malcolm McLaren, a horrible man, couldn't get all the visas for the horrible band he mananged, the Sex Pistols. (Don't fight me. I was there. I bought
Never Mind
at Positively 4th street.) Costello's drummer, Pete Thomas, wore a T-shirt that said "Thanks Malc" and no one knew what it meant.
Anyway. I have lots of new music and things from the last 15 years in genres I'm just discovering. And it's rare I listen to it. I stopped listening to music on a daily basis about a year ago. I thought I would fill the Fred with music but it turns out I want to live in silence.
This, I hope, changes. Perhaps with The Last House.
Speaking of which.
I saw a tweet the other day from the local activists and DSA enthusiasts who were announcing a door-knocking tour to get support from their Tax the Rich! Initiative. All these carpetbagger theater-kids eager for state-enforced property redistribution. Like the old attitude about porn: they canât identity what ârichâ is but they know it when they see it. Iâm just glad I have calluses on my hands from lifting weights, because when the new Pol-Potheads send the intellectuals to the killing fields I can hide my glasses and turn my hands palm up.
Kidding. But hereâs the thing: Minneapolis is the only place around here where I can get a house that has the old solid qualities I love. I have always loved this city and boosted it and championed its history and architecture and uniqueness . . . and now it seems like a tarpit.
The news is full of people stunned by their property tax increases. I'm sure they went up at Jasperwood, but we had a fantastically low mortgage payment. item.description:
THE CASE OF THE TARRY SHOEPRINTS
HAS BEEN SOLVED
If you recall, Iâd seen footprints in the elevator lobby, and noticed more in the garage. What seemed odd: they went away from the elevator. I traced them upstairs to my floor, down the hall, to the welcome mat of a guy on my floor I know. I ran into him just now on the last walk out for the night, and I had to ask.
Whereupon he began scrolling through his phone to show me a picture of the shoes. Heâd had them in storage, bagged, for several months, and had taken them out to wear as part of a Halloween costume. When he was walking to his car he noticed that his gait felt odd - spongy - and when he looked at his shoes he saw that the soles had broken down, the chemical bonds loosened, the entire sole turning into a thick liquid. Whereupon he returned to his flat, shoes in hand, rueing the mess, and chose different, non-deteriorating shoes.
I said it was cheap Chinese krep, and he said no, naming a high-quality brand with a good reputation. Anyway, now I know. After I talked to him Birch and I went out front for the final wee, and ran into the lady whose dog has continence issues. Asked if his bladder was holding together better and indeed, it was. On the way up, ran into The Attractive Divorcee, who asked how the seizures were, and I said, stupidly, âfine. Oh you mean the dog. Also fine.â
Once back upstairs I googled the shoes, and was rewarded with a flood of stories about people complaining that this particular brand of shoe had a tendency to deteriorate. AI summary: âEcco shoe soles disintegrate primarily due to a chemical process called hydrolysis, which breaks down the polyurethane (PU) material used in the midsoles and outsoles.â Storage seems to accelerate the problem.
And that was a day at the Fred. Cloudy but also warm. The water is still open.
I am fiercely grateful for this place.
Tuesday was a peculiar day. Let me fill you in on the odd details:
The internet worked
The credit card was accepted at the gas pump, which also worked
The internet at the gym worked
Apple iCloud and the app store all worked
I was able to connect to my bank and transfer money
All of this seemed to be anomalous. Yes, there were outages, and yes, there seem to be a lot of them. As I tweeted earlier:
Half of jittery twitter is saying surely somethingâs about to kick off. Defenses and systems are being probed, more attacks are coming. Possibly, but if youâre planning on bringing down the electrical grid, maybe youâd want to keep your powder dry and not get everyoneâs attention by crashing Office for a day.
No, I think itâs something thatâs almost worse, in its own way: complex systems that have been inadequately maintained or updated, AND / OR, something something AI is being added to the systems AND / OR autonomous skynet agents have been unleashed to wreak general and specific havoc.
All of the above is possible. All of the above is probably likely, but you can also look at this like the UAP / UFO Drone Swarm from last year.
The frequency illusion, also known as the BaaderâMeinhof phenomenon, is a cognitive bias in which a person notices a specific concept, word, or product more frequently after recently becoming aware of it.
The name "BaaderâMeinhof phenomenon" was coined in 1994 by Terry Mullen in a letter to the St. Paul Pioneer Press. The letter describes how, after mentioning the name of the German militant group BaaderâMeinhof once, he kept noticing it. This led to other readers sharing their own experiences of the phenomenon, leading it to gain recognition. It was not until 2005, when Stanford linguistics professor Arnold Zwicky wrote about this effect on his blog, that the name "frequency illusion" was coined.
Oddly enough I donât think Iâll start seeing Zwickys anywhere. I wish this was called something other than Baader-Meinhof Syndrome, but I will always think that leftist revolutionaries had robbed a bank and killed someone on behalf of Karl and Vladimir.
I tried to find the Pioneer Press article, but itâs paywalled, and newspaper.com has only a few issues of the paper, stopping at 31. Oh look, itâs a picture section.
Hey, thatâs H. G. Wells! Computer, colorize
Do you know what he sounded like? I have it around here somewhere . . . okay, 14TB archive > Audio > OTR > Misc > Misc2000-2006 . . . ah.
Nice job, Orson
Anyway.
Daughter and I were texting about the imminent Nov. 17th internet shutdown, something the ill-informed socials were passing along and adding to the reasons not to get out of bed or find a job. Memes were exchanged. This morning she sends me the news story about the NSA having internal internet problems, and I thought: NoSuchAgency puts out a press release that itâs been compromised?
Apparently
so. Odd.
While at the gym I saw two tweets from people who said they knew someone who knew someone who said the power would shut off in the three days, or maybe for three days, maybe for 90, and this was intentional. The reasons seemed vague, but I take it that the Powers wanted to dissolve society, reconstitute it along serfish lines while they lived in luxury in their emergency bunkers, and then emerge into a world where nothing works anymore because society broke down. This was so the corporations could complete their control of everyoneâs movements and thoughts. So youâd better
stock up on water.
Yes, rich people look at the fireplace at night while swirling a brandy and think âitâs not a question of whether I
should
kill half the planet, itâs
how
.â The people who want to kill half the planet for the betterment of . . . of
things
, I guess, are not the rich people, but poor corporals with middling art talent, or mediocre-minded Marxists.
It's an odd combination of thoughts: no one has freedom anymore because of billionaires and capitalism. Also, billionaires want to take away your freedom to do and say what you want. The capitalist hellscape means corporations don't care about you at all, but just want to force money out of your pores. Also, they are keenly bent on making your life worse, so you cannot afford to buy anything. Also, x.com is a nazi hellhole because a billionaire

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
Sometimes I tire
of supplying pictures of the actual world and want some idealized landscapes with a Bacchanian rite. Thatâs a work by Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes, a plien-air Neoclassist. I don't know how I stumbled upon this - might have been while doing some "research" for a column I did about changes to the National Gallery in London. (The changes are not reassuring. More modern voices! Change the mission for the new audience! You know,
the people who don't go to museums
. It's like changing NFL rules to attract people who abhor kinetic collisions, or replacing the adagio of a symphony with a Jay-Z track. I mention that particular performer because the gym was playing one of his "songs," and it consisted of the same motif repeated without alteration or modulation for five minutes, during which Mr. -Z spoke rapidly about some disconcerting events that had befallen him.
Right,
that
song.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.

you realize how much you know about things you never think about. The opportunity never arises to say "oh, I know what that is." You grow up in a particular era, you become accustomed to the visual language of the time. Things that are iconic, as they say. They didnât mean anything a hundred years ago, and a hundred years from now they wonât mean anything. Does this mean all trans-identified men are predators? Of course not. Should trans people be discriminated against when it comes to housing or employment? Of course not. Should trans people be stripped of their human rights, or denied personal safety? Again: of course not.

item.description:
I'd live there.

I vibe-coded an app

If there is a dining room in The Last House, then it would be reserved for the evening meal. Breakfast and lunch in the sunlit kitchen nook, dinner at a proper table. Why, I can just see me sitting there, having a civilized dinner:
=

This all presumes a lot, of course. Iâm heading down to look at the Lake City place tomorrow. Uncle Gary says he has some nice old homes in Minneapolis at a reasonable price, but Iâm curious about the neighborhood. And when I look, I get this:
That is half the size and 85K more.
I will open a vein first.

I think people believe Lake City is a hamlet in the middle of nowhere instead of a small town with bars, restaurants (one with a bowling alley!), a new library, a new fitness center, a Mayo Clinic, and so on. Also, a Lake. Village green with gazebo.
You know,
Willoughby
! No hold on, not Willoughby. Or maybe Willoughby.
I donât know.
I DONâT KNOW.
Hereâs what happened Saturday. Last night I wrote:
Perhaps if I write about this
I can explain it. I think I had a 24-hour bug and it led to a mild dissociative episode. Something new!
The bug thing was interesting. When I was picking up Birchâs meds, the pharmacist was coughing a lot, and as I left Target I heard other people coughing, and thought: well, it is that time. When was my last cold? Ah yes: got the ague good and hard in Walbers during the stay when I got The Letter, and ended up with a productive cough that stayed with me for three months.
The next day I suddenly felt a particular kind of scratchiness in the throat that always presages a cold, and thought back to the coughing pharmacist. Of all people from whom to catch a cold, a pharmacist. Well, here we go, hope itâs not the strain that laid the Giant Swede low for weeks. He had his kids to bring soup and check in on him. Hell, his Ex probably brought food and checked in on him.
I took Zinc and resigned myself. Realized my pneumonia shot was probably due. Made an appointment for that.
After I wrote that segment about houses and moving and the matter of the Fred being a transitional place, a decompression chamber, I went to sleep and had what seemed like hours of messy, unlikeable dreams.
Fever dreams.
I was standing on a street corner in Lake City looking at the vast Mississippi, stuck, alone, nothing but the great gray water and little me, some sort of purgatory, not a real place. Then dreams of houses going wrong, houses with tilted staircases, houses with slanted floors, then small houses in barren tracts with muttering unfriendly neighbors. I woke, uneasy, made breakfast, and started to feel ill. For the next six hours I had grotesque stomach pains. Decided I might cure it with exertion, so took Birch for a long walk. As we walked outside I heard this tapping sound in the breezeway, somewhat random, unfamiliar, unnerving.
When we got back, Fred Base One seemed entirely false and empty, not my home at all but some arrangement of items I had made to convince myself I had a home, and it wasnât that at all. All these familiar items from the Real Lost Home were just empty items disconnected from meaning and history. It was just an impersonal box. I would be gone soon and it would all be filled up by someone else, and I would leave no trace. It wasnât mine.
But I had no idea where I would go next. Lake City: the Lonely Exile, like decamping to the Hebrides except Iâd be heading south. The Richfield rambler: alone on some block still driving around the same old places, sandwiched between strangers. I thought of standing by the Oak Island Water Feature talking to the next door neighbor over the fence. I miss that guy. Why Am I Not There? Ah: right: I was pushed out of that life. I felt sick again. Put the dog in the car and walked to Centennial and did another long walk, breathed in and out, deep, realized what old memory had been awoken: living in the high rise in college, disconnected from my old neighborhood and old haunts, completely alienated from place and self. Iâd had the same stomach problems then, but for weeks. I had seen a doctor and was informed that I was probably an unhappy young man in college.
They saw a lot of that.
Once I realized this I could start to connect again, and by the time I got home I felt better. After a nap, mostly normal. In the evening, work and a movie, but not serious work. The movie was that one where Barbara Stanwyck is all confident and happy but then she falls apart and is prone to outbursts. That one.
I remembered the term âdissociative episodeâ later while I was getting the bag of dog food out of the trunk, and googled it. Trust me, I had the mildest example possible. But it was one of those strip-to-the-core moments that makes you realize there are levels of unhappiness you havenât accessed yet, which seems . . . RIDICULOUS. I mean A) Iâve been doing okay here, and B) Whatâs left, for Godâs sake?
Well, a bad patch, perhaps. A time when the Cantâs ânâ Shantâs side of the ledger is overbalanced. Every option just seems pathetic. I just want to go home.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
item.description:
I hope you had a fine
weekend. Mine was busy. For a while I briefly considered parting my hair on the side, but then discarded the idea. I also spent some time watching the dog for signs of listlessness, since I'd given him the new tranks. He was not listless. I wrote a lot, watched some interesting television programs, and, while studying the antecedents and source material of those retro-atomic AI videos we may or may not have discussed, realized that AI music makes me feel anxious and itchy. I'm talking about the mood-music / easy-listening "Luxury Jazz" that copies mid-century hi-fi swank. It's as if it sets the two hemispheres of the brain against each other. When I listened to an example of the real thing, it was like drinking fresh cold water after an hour of sucking on a paper towel soaked with Windex.
Lots of pursuits, in other words. I'm writing this on a Sunday night, ready for the chores and deadlines of the week to come, but man, am I glad that weekend is over. Saturdays are always bad. This one had a flavor of bad I haven't tasted since 1982. But that's for tomorrow. Now I give you what I wrote on Friday, with the now-traditional Old-Fashioned 11 PM Relaxation Writing Session. (Wedge of orange to garnish. Delicious.)
There are many good aspects
to this life. I can take a nap without guilt. I still set an alarm, though. Too much nap, and you drag. I get 6 and a half hours of sleep overnight, then 40 - 55 minutes between the utterly useless hour of 4 PM - 5 PM, and this keeps me reasonably sharp for evening work. The period after the nap feels cleanly demarcated from the time that went before. Everything resets - mood, energy, determination. Occasionally, though, it goes wrong. I jerked out of a nap because Iâd had an image in a dream that woke me up: a view of a glass in my hand slamming down on a table. It was one of my new glasses with the pebbled texture. There was something final and angry about the action, and I snapped away. Checked the clock: ehhhhhh. Iâd been out for 17 minutes.
But. Sometimes just entering REM is enough to recharge. I wondered if the glass-slam was my brainâs way of interpreting something else that jerked me awake. As I may have said, I nap wearingAirPods with white noise, and if Iâm dreaming when the alarm goes off, there is a moment where everyone falls silent and the action stops and everyone behaves with hushed confusion like a movie shoot after the director yells CUT out of nowhere. Silence, then the alarm. The brain rewrites the nap script the second the white noise cuts out.
Well, weâre up. Too early to start dinner. Donât want to sit at the computer and continue the day's rote work, which is renumbering the navigation for the 1930s B&W World site. Thereâs 12 minutes of daylight left. Letâs go for a walk.
I let him choose which direction: the old-style clockwise path that goes around Sunderwood, around the playground, then through Pentagon Park, or the Widdershins route. Today he chose the clockwise option. Halfway through he picked up an enormous stick and gave no sign of letting it go, and he trotted with the log half the distance back, course-correcting so he could deposit it at the auxiliary stick deposit spot.
This was the second stick of the day! O what luck! Post-gym we did the Centennial walk, and he dropped his stick to go say hello to the nice lady who works at FedEx, and sometimes just goes out the back door to stand there and bask in the sun. When we walked past she said âhello Birchâ so we went over to chat. Edinaâs Number One Dog.
Since it was Friday, I had pizza. Since the freezer compartment is small, there's no room for a frozen pizza, so Fridays I go to Target. Used to have four or five in the downstairs freezer, couple pep-saus for me, couple veg / pineapple for her, and I will go to my grave remembering the slight resistance of the freezer door when you pulled it, the big nail-and-screw organizer on the gray counter, the picture of a Texaco station leaning against the wall, the big COKE circle, the painting her mother did, the stack of neon-hued yardsticks piled up from years of the Fair shows. The very thought of "getting a pizza from the freezer" turns on the room in the mental holodeck. Joy. Anyway, got the pizza, and didn't mind the trip. Why, I had a Target Circle Deal: buy $30 worth of food, and get $5 off! Careful shopping got me enough food to last the rest of the week, but of course I will go grocery shopping.
Why? It gets me out, I suppose. Consumes time. You can talk to people and it's a great day when I can talk to someone.
Yes yes I should be out there signing up for improv classes or Adult Education or Pickleball or something, but thereâs the matter of the dog-shaped boat anchor chewing the leg of the entryway table the last time he was left alone. I have new tranks to keep him from chewing through the pocket doors or madly scratching the walls looking for me, but they donât bring him down far enough. So if Iâm just going to hiber-hermit life going forward foreswearing the suburban bustle that occasionally produces Human Interaction, why not move to the distant lakeside town? I could join the historical society and hang out at the neighborhood pub.
I mean: $265K.
You know what that gets you in the city? A rude shack in a part of town where the streets twinkle in the morn when the sun hits the broken car window glass and property taxes of 8K.
Hereâs something in the area Iâve been considering. It's one hundred and ten thousand dollars more than the house above.
I do not know what is going on with this kitchen:
Original ornamental wood over the sink. Probably the original door knobs. One metal sheet over the counters, stovetop controls to the left of the burners.
It has a shed.
If I go south to the river, the small town, I can have a proper office instead of a small bedroom with tiny rambler corner windows.
There are weeks when I think: yes yes of course, RICHFIELD! And there are weeks when it seems like that means living in a fargin' crackerbox at the periphery of the life I loved and lost.
And then there are nights like this, when I think: this year was a transition, and a good one. Familiar. The environs are connected to the old life but it wasnât anything we shared; this was always the Land of Errands. Instead of driving north to go home, now I go south. The Fred is a place through which people pass, each at a different pace. I stand on the balcony at night enjoying a lease violation and look at the lights, hear the constant white noise of the Seagate factory, and think: it was never forever. I was lucky that it was so different and interesting that it gave me a clear demarcation.
Staying around here is settling, sinking.
Leaving is . . . courageous?
Iâd make a rule: go up to the Cities on Wednesday and Sunday, see the lads. Itâs only 87 minutes. It's ten minutes to Red Wing with a Target.
A porch. Summer. Crickets. The river a few blocks away.
Everything so different that I can settle into the rest of my days in proper exile.
Maybe thatâs what my dreams are telling me. The glass slams down on the table with a sharp rap.
Wake up.
In keeping with our Monday tradition, which became a "tradition" for reasons I can't recall and probably don't matter, we continue with our Monday trademark. For this year we'll do 1936.
The trademark for Republic Ictures:
They started up in 1935
, gathering all the Poverty Row studios into one brand. Republic would make over 1,000 movies before it closed in '67.
I'm always up for a good hell-noir:
Hey! Wow!
I had no idea! Okay, what do we have?
Let me just give you the basics of the first part, with a series of relevant frames.
We meet our protagonist, whoâs in his bed wearing a shirt and tie, with a cat.
The building's seductive custodianess comes in and cleans the apartment.
He throws her out. Then he checks a piece of paper, and gets ready to go on a job.
He feeds the cat.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
item.description:
The sight that makes you sag
inside, just a little.
If you know, you know.
If soon it does get white, I'll have to think about decorations. Some Christmas-colored lights on the balcony, sure. A tree? I could get all-new decorations. Not sure what I kept, but they're packed away at Zork Storage. I like the idea of a clean install, since all the ornaments have stories and all the stories are dead.
Dry and cold.
Wrote a ton this morning, did a Substack, laid out three pages for next week, then off to the gym. Blue Oyster Cult was playing in the locker room, which made me smile, and also made me angry, recollecting the dinner we had with Buck Dharma and his wife one summer evening in Minneapolis, in the bygone life. Little triggers everywhere. Still warm enough for a post-workout walk down to Centennial Lakes, and at Birch's watering hole there was the fellow I ran into a few weeks ago, the Similarily Situated Recent Divorced Writer Guy. This was good, since I hadn't had a conversation with anyone for a few days, and we swapped tales. I enjoy talking to people at length and the opportunities are few these days, so it charges all the batteries. Target to get dog-head meds, home for tea, nap. Fish-and-chips dinner with a spot of HP sauce, another packet liberated from the buffet at the Backrooms Hotel at Heathrow. Did the Aftershow with Duane, and then an evening of work. Two columns due tomorrow.
Anything else? Oh, always! So much more. Apparently I have to go into Discus tonight and ban another troll. I wonder what sort of mental energy it takes to tell yourself that everyone is struck to the pith of their marrow by your ripostes, when everyone either ignores or laughs. It's such a joyless, bilious existence, showing up under fake names and telling people to die.
Speaking of joy:
If you're a Substack subscriber, you recall this fellow from Wednesday, where I discussed the yin-yang attitude about hedonism in the 80s and 90s. The Captain was all about having big Rum Fun, but was obliged to shout "Responsibly!" now and then. You'll note his aides have banners that reinforce the idea. He's running for President because we're at the 2008 Democratic National Convention.
(I should note that the Wednesday entry is loosey-goosey, expanding on material removed from the Mon or Fri columns.)
Anyway, I was hanging around with a Miami Herald journalist who also had been sent to write humor, and we would shout "Responsibly!" at relevant intervals. I wondered if he remembered, so I wrote him last night. He did! We hadn't talked since his book about living with an old dog, which I enjoyed. He also noted with astonishment that he's about to turn 80.
I am not making that up.
Doesn't look a day over 58.
I was finishing some additions
to the 1980s TV ad section, and found this 1988 ad for Southern Comfort. This was not an unusual plot or setting. The nostalgia for old classic American forms had been going on since
Happy Days
, but people still thought there were classic diners like this out there in the heartland, complete with Vic-Tayback types working the grill.
I don't think modern ads would choose "quit your job and go drinking" for the plot, but it worked back then.
Here's the shot I liked. You know itâs a real authentic Diner because thereâs a hardhat guy standing outside with his leg up on the bumper of his Ford pickup.
Let's see if we can upscale that a bit.
Not really.
I didnât read this is as a diner, though. Thatâs a gas station. It has the lines of a Moderne station, and you can read the left side as a hint of the bays.
Of course I had to find it. Googleâs AI was confident that it was in New Orleans, since thatâs what the ad was all about. Google AI was not correct. When I pressed a bit more, it said, with complete and total confidence:
This restaurant is actually not located in or around New Orleans at all.
While the commercial was produced to promote the New Orleans spirit of Southern Comfort, this specific scene was filmed at the iconic 66 Diner located at 1405 Central Ave NE, Albuquerque, New Mexico.
Oh! Great. Letâs take a look.
Remind me again how this is the super-intelligence that will conquer humanity
But wait. Letâs go to the dinerâs website. The history page says it burned down in 1995. The building above is a newer version. The old Diner was once . . . a gas station.
So is this how you spend you time
?
Yes, but it took five minutes. Then you do something else for the next five or ten, and at the end of the day you have all sorts of fun stuff rattling around your brain. It's not as if I'm going to overhear anyone saying "I saw that 1988 Southern Comfort commercial, and I just wish I knew the story behind those exterior location shots." But one can hope.
I bought online a nice old street clock, the type that used to stand on the corner on a pole like a streetlight. The online listing mentioned a glowing dial. When I got it, I realized that it glowed because of radium, so this was a big mistake. I would have to dispose of it in pieces, surreptitiously. I was all the more irritated with myself when I remembered that I had bought one of these things before and had the same problem. How many radium-affected antique street clocks were there on eBay?
Mr. Felts. NARVEL Felts. I don't remember this one at all,
Wikipedia
:
Albert Narvel Felts (born November 11, 1938) is an American country music and rockabilly singer. Known for his soaring tenor and high falsetto, Felts enjoyed his greatest success during the 1970s, most famously 1975's "Reconsider Me".
It's a scant bio for a long career.
That will do. Hope you enjoyed the week! Substack up at 11 for paying customers, and we'll all meet here next Monday for more of the same, except completely different.

item.description:
The downpour abates,
and youâve a moment to dash out in the drizzle before the next rain-laden cloud lumbers over and opens up. All day, on and off. For the morning walk, a light mist that didnât deter Birch from his irrigations and deposits; after the gym, a certain sparkle in the air, like walking through effervescence.
We went down to the spot where he drinks -
- and noted how much had fallen away.
Well,
I
noted. He noticed a dead squirrel and was intent on bringing it home. He contented himself with a stick at least six feet long, which he carried with the usual jaunty pride until it tangled in the leash, then got between my legs and snapped in half. He looked at it:
oh itâs not as good now BUT itâs easier to carry so hurrah.
On we went, pausing every 15 seconds so he could bite the stick into smaller segments until it was no longer an object of interest, and was dropped and forgotten.
This was after the gym, which was no fun because
A)
the back has been screaming all day from yesterdayâs workout (as I have noted, I work out so I have a good explanation for the aches and pains of Advanced Age) and
B)
there's this little idiot who sets herself between a bench and the weight rack and does one exercise every nine minutes, spending the rest of the time tikking the tok. I finally said something today after she had stopped and I could replace my 30s:
âThis isnât a very good place to set up,â I said, gesturing at the weight rack. She gave me a blank look, pointed to her earbuds, and said something in Spanish and then went back to the critical visions on the phone. Sigh.
C)
The weird big guy who asked about Halloween Houses last week was in the locker room and started doing a dance to the song on the speakers. It was like watching a potbellied Frankenstein try to moonwalk. On the other hand, I got a hearty âhello Jamesâ from Mo and Alyssia, and itâs always nice to have someone say hello to you and say your name. Otherwise after a while you just float away and evaporate.
As for the rest of the day: O the boring things I could relate! And probably will! I decided to iron all the sweaters and shirts, and arrange the closet for full-on fall and certain winter. This made me feel absolutely no better about my closet than before, since the closets are the main flaw of Fred Base One. Thereâs no room for a bureau, so I have no drawers. Just fabric boxes and hangars. But at least things are neater and organized. Whew! Wipe the sweat from the brow and let the heart get down to resting rate after that! On to the next boring thing: fixing old websites. This usually means undoing previous bad decisions and making new bad decisions. But I shored up a lot of things, and was once again heartened by the quantity of material yet to be released. All for free!
Yeah, about that. Weâll get to that.
Dinner was the fifth meal Iâve gotten out of the Aldi 8-skewer marinated chicken pack ($7.99), and this pleased me to no end. Food is my greatest expense, aside from all the regular recurring bills. Iâve started feeding the receipts into the Monarch money-management app, which totals everything up and breaks out the categories and says âyes, food is your greatest expense.â Helpful. Finished with a lovely salad, then headed out for a walk in the drizzle. The three sisters are totally bare:
The evening has mysteries we will never know:
Back up to Fred Base One for the evening work. I stopped in the package room and saw a big box: ELECTRIC FIREPLACE. Fake, in other words. This was the sort of day that makes you want to stay inside and have a cup of tea and sit by the fire, if you had one, which of course I donât anymore. I I probably don't deserve one. It is entirely apt and symbolic of the Current Life that there are two fireplaces at the Fred, and neither produce any heat at all.
I donât know why I clipped this, but it provided an interesting prompt right away:
What? Australians?
That was
a British joke. Says the link:
The line was also used in Australia, in much the same context, although appearances of it in newspapers there post-date those in Britain and the USA.
The phrase was popularized by Tommy Trinder (1909-1989), a well-known and well-liked English comedian (seen here with Phil Silvers).
The article, it should be noted, does not have a picture of Trinder with Phil Silvers. The line with its parenthetical aside can be found in two other locations, neither of which have a picture of Phil Silvers.
I did find the picture, though.
About Mr. Trinder:
Thomas Edward Trinder CBE (24 March 1909 â 10 July 1989) was an English stage, screen and radio comedian whose catchphrase was "You lucky people!". Described by cultural historian Matthew Sweet as "a cocky, front-of-cloth variety turn", he was one of the United Kingdom's foremost entertainers during the Second World War.
Heeeeereâs Tommy!
All the bios seem to find this important, for a reason we'll get to in a moment:
In 1941, he appeared in
Eating Out with Tommy Trinde
r, a public information film promoting wartime British Restaurants.
Can we? We can:
The British Restaurants were a wartime experiment:
British Restaurants were communal kitchens created in 1940 during the Second World War to help people who had been bombed out of their homes, had run out of ration coupons or otherwise needed help. In 1943, 2,160 British Restaurants served 600,000 very inexpensive meals a day. They were disbanded in 1947. There was a political dimension as well, as the Labour Party saw them as a permanent solution to equalising consumption across the class line and guaranteeing a nourishing diet to all.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
item.description:
That was last week.
It's not like that anymore. It looked like this at Centennial Lakes, where I went to vote.
I was headed to the polling place when I noticed there was a polling place around the corner, in the Fire Station. Hmm. It's closer. This is probably it! I went inside, and told the lady my last name.
"James," she said, automatically. Okay well that's nice. She couldn't find me in the system, but I said I had moved - oh, well, you'll have to register. Fine! Over to the other table. Gave her my name. "Oh, I read you all the time!" she said. And that's nice too. I suppose my demographic was election judges, or people who could be, or admired them. If they're newspaper readers of a certain age, they might think well of Amy Klobuchar, running for Guber, because they read her father in the paper. I like Amy, because I think she's old-school DFL / Nordic-model social compact / Wendy Anderson holding up a fish Minnesota liberal at odds with the DSA Metro surge, but I don't know if that particular ideological levee is made of concrete or sand. I disagreed with her father on a lot of things (not that he noticed or cared) and he was never particularly friendly when I ran into him on the radio station, but he did love Minnesota in that way we all did, once.
Anyway, the poll official couldn't get my address to take, and it turned out I was in the wrong place.
"But I'm just around the corner!" I said, adding "at the Fred!" Somehow Fred status was not enough. As it turned out this polling location was a temporary one, used by people who had gone to the Library before it was razed. The Library is about six blocks from Centennial Lakes, but I am not yet wise in the ways of Edina, so fine, no problem. Off to . . .
It was 1 PM, and empty. I voted, and was given a sticker. I always feel like I'm getting one of those balloons you got at the pediatrician that said "From My Doctor For Being Good" even if you'd screamed and cried when you got a shot. The man at the ballot-reading machine said "Thank you for voting," and I wanted to say "You're welcome! I wrote in Hitler for every office!" because voting's all well and good, but it does matter
what
you vote for, no?
Thank you for doing your part to advance every cause to which I am opposed with every molecule of my being!
But I get it. This is how we solve our problems, or at least produce a new group of officials who will take a different approach to not solving our problems.
I was watching that video of the raving student who attacked the Jewish student for noting wryly that her ordinary garb would not be popular in Islamic countries, and she was quite clear at the end in expressing her desire to kill the Jew, and heck, anyone else who's Jew-adjacent. If you're sufficiently online you see the
lol kys
a lot. These people do not thank you for voting.
Which brings us to the matter of the Bloody T-Shirt. My feed has a series of headlines about the Minnesota Election Judge who was wearing a white shirt with a bloodstain. It was thought to be a reference to Charlie Kirk, and as such, some people were outraged. I'm not using the word lightly, since
everyone is always outraged
these days. It was later revealed that the judge was a Republican, and it was a Halloween T-shirt that's been around for a while. There was a
similar controversy in Tucson last year, this time concerning some math teachers.
I found the shirt for sale online, and it appears to preceded Kirk's assassination.
I'm not sure what the shirt is supposed to mean, except that the wearer has used violence to overcome a difficult situation. As far as I can tell, it's not a callback to some gory movie, or a reference to some quip in a book or a meme. It's just a bloody shirt with a phrase.
Interpreting it as a Kirk reference is entirely reasonable, though. If you saw all the Kirkiversary posts on X, or all the pictures people gleefully posted of themselves wearing white "Freedom" shirts with a bloodstain to indicate the bullet wound, of course that's what you'd think. I expect the old lady didnât know, not being terminally online, but you can absolutely understand why someone would conclude it was one of innumerable happy recreations of Kirk's death.
The people who celebrate don't bother me as much as the people who wouldn't do it themselves, but, y'know,
kinda understand
why someone would?
Anyway. Wet day all around, no let up. A damp-dog-smell day. Gym, a bit of shopping, mindful of the new budget, no frills. Leftover Chicken Burger dinner for supper, absolutely delicious with Lundsnbyerly's Sriracha Mustard sauce and a big salad of spinach and something else that has a bitter taste so you say "it's not iceberg, must be healthy." I finished two projects I'd been picking away at all day, two 14-page websites on 40s culture. Now listening to swank French downbeat chill sung by some husky chanteuse who's been bruised by l'amour but is wiser for it. I think. She could be complaining about the historical trends in petrol prices, but probably not.
Ah: just translated the line she repeats, and it's "I don't remember taking this path."
People say Reddit is a cesspool, and that's not quite accurate. There are many useful, factual, smart, reasoned subreddits. A lot depends on the moderators. You can tell a moderator has the cliched Reddit mindset when you see a rule like "4. Transwomen are women" and it's a subreddit devoted to fountain pens.
I was reading about the Paris riots in a subreddit devoted to Lost Architecture. As with 2020, you are sternly discouraged from mourning property destruction, which only shows you are missing the real issue.
Don't get me wrong, bro, I'm totally on board with burning museums, if they're the ones that need burning.
This one is fun, because it contains accusations of "state worship" from people who want to hand the state all sorts of sweeping powers, providing the state's objectives align with theirs.
Again, the reassurance:
don't get me wrong I totally understand burning down a building that has an office where people make money in a way that abrades my ideology, but City Hall?
This is the moderate view.
On X, the purest expression of the argument:
Of course the local resident and the city's money could be traced back to stolen colonial wealth, since that term has been redefined to encompass all money not yet in the hands of the State.
I also enjoy reading the local subreddits
to see how people frame and discuss current events. Nothing is ever surprising. You will have someone say something sane - always preceded by establishing bonafides: âIâm a lifelong socialist and F Trump,â which means the arguments are meant in good faith, not from a PLACE OF HATE. This just means itâs generally ignored or quietly downvoted.
So: there was a big screaming mess at the Union Depot at The Bundle Halal Fall Event. Private party, lots of vendors, religious requirement for being a vendor. There was some sort of dispute that caused everyone to stampede for the exits. This slotted alongside the series of shootings around town at places and events not previously known for shootings, but if you note the rise in clan / gang warfare, youâre being jerked around by bots. The following replies are an almost perfect Reddit sequence:
The last one shifts the blame where all the right-thinking people know blame resides, so the matter is closed.
Elsewhere, in Dinkytown, a massive police presence. There have been many instances in the last few years when the police have had to flood into the neighborhood and break up late-night mobs of Youts who do not live in Dinkytown.

item.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
item.description:
Dark and portentous day.
Rain from the start, mean rain, but not cold. You look out at the trees on the boulevard and realize theyâre all bare. Everythingâs bare. The curtain went down and the stage was reset.
I watched the storms on my weather app to see when thereâs be a break for Birch to do what he needed to do. Or, I could look out the window. When we went out in the drizzle there was no one around. The machinery wasnât running. Sunderwood Park has been completely churned up; all the grass and flora and weeds and such are plowed over, an dark sea of mud.
Did afternoon errands, and felt that I should be stockpiling, as the governments have been advising. It's amusing, because I used to have everything set aside for whatever emergency might beset the land. Turns out I was prepping for the wrong apocalypse. I still have dehydrated foods, but most of the Crisis Equipment went in the estate sale, I think. So I'm at Targe today, looking at sensible canned goods, like tinned chicken "in water," which I assume they have to add as a frank admission. You would never order chicken in a restaurant and ask the waiter "is that
in water
?"
Oh yes sir all of our chicken is in water.
I would never eat that stuff. I haven't room for serious supplies. I bought three packets of sriracha-infused tuna, which I use for sandwiches. I am woefully unprepared and feel uncomfortable about it.
Why? What's going to happen? Nothing is going to happen. Right?
In the evening

âDonât worry,â I said. âItâs not fireworks. Itâs just gunfire.â He wanted to make haste back to Fred Base One, and so we did. A neighbor from down the hall, Reed, was getting something from a car under the canopy, and he saw us and called out HELLO BIRCH!

Thick black muddy prints in the lobby. Who could be so careless?

I had the epiphany: these are going away from the apartment.
I followed the trail to the end of the parking garage.
Strange.
And then it got stranger. As I was walking back to Fred Base One, I saw the footprints in
my hallway
. They stopped
here
.

HOW DO YOU LEAVE YOUR HOUSE WITH TARRY SHOES
Anyway, based on my chat with Reed,
everyone is talking about this.

You miserable juvenile legacy-trashing idiots
There is, in the history of
Star Trek
, no greater missed opportunity than Season 4 of

It is located in a valley carved by the outflow of an enormous glacial lake at the end of the last Ice Age. The lake formed when the Mississippi, a successor to the glacial river, was partially dammed by a delta from a tributary stream and spread out across the ancient valley.

Okay, rewind. The police came because four Youts from down the street had walked through the alley, thought it would be fun to pick up a piece of wood that had a nasty 16â spike driven through it, and throw it over the Swedeâs garage. shape
of things, and perhaps have seen the seminal films. They can talk about the studio system and the rise of the young directors in the 70s. But I find it hard to convince them to watch old movies. the Spielberg version, doesnât seem dated at all, even though itâs (sigh) 21 years old. Even in 1977 the 1953 War seemed to be from another era.

Classic example (sorry) of having to distinguish the artist from the art. I learned something I didnât know, which is always good. Consider these two:
You may know the couple. Mr. & Mrs. Lavoisier. Scientists.
Consider their work:
Lavoisier is noted for his discovery of the role oxygen plays in combustion, opposing the prior phlogiston theory of combustion. He named oxygen (1778), recognizing it as an element, and also recognized hydrogen as an element (1783).
By using more precise measurements than previous experimenters, he confirmed the developing theory that, although matter in a closed system may change its form or shape, its mass always remains the same (now known as the law of conservation of mass), which led to the development of the balanced physical and chemical reaction equations that we still use today.
Lavoisier helped construct the metric system, wrote the first extensive list of elements, in which he predicted the existence of silicon, and helped to reform chemical nomenclature. (1787)
His wife and laboratory assistant, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, became a renowned chemist in her own right, and worked with him to develop the metric system of measurements.
Her individual bio's impressive, too.
Remarkable people. The intellectual vanguard of a sophisticated, inquisitive culture.But that culture changed with remarkable speed and ferocity.
At the height of the French Revolution, he was charged with tax fraud and selling adulterated tobacco and was guillotined despite appeals to spare his life in recognition of his contributions to science. A year and a half later, he was exonerated by the French government.

EARLY AM
Woke without the usual enthusiasm. Sometimes on Tuesday I wake thinking of the things I set aside to make the day good, and they give me a smile. Today, nah. Meh morn. Open the shade: gray day. Check the temp: cold. The warm weather was gone for good, and I knew that yesterday. When we got back from the morning trip to fertilize the world I had this strange flashback, a mood of emptiness and solitude, something that had struck me sharp and hard when I was in London a year ago. Right before the letter. A sense of weary vacancy.
Went through the day as usual: work on the site in the AM, edit the Substack, do the art, then something new and different: I ironed lots of pants. O the excitement. Well, colder weather, best start dressing in good pants and nice sweaters, for some reason. Lunch was leftover pasta with the Trader Joe's hot Italian sausage, and they're not kidding: every bite a firecracker. Rather pointless. Gym, a quiet walk in Centennial, some comtemplative time in the chair by the lake, then the weekly big Target trip: get a bag of dog food and some chew sticks, can't run out of those. When I got home to the apartment in the late afternoon light, all cloudy outside the big windows, I felt that London feel again. Well! Nap. That always resets the day.
5:37 PM Sitting outside at the Yard,
which is the dog's yard of Yard, watching him work on the big log he dragged in from the field, studying the Grok responses to some necessary questions. Pretty much what I expected. A lot depends on the blood work, it seems.
I note that I have a badge for a missed call: it's the vet. He left a message. Says the blood work looks good, wants to talk about the sedation options I'd discussed. I'd missed the call because, at 4:35, Birch was seizing. This is absolutely horrible and unequivocably bad news, unspinnable, with only one resolution.
The MST, we were told, was 2 to 6 months with medication only. The upper range is 12 months, which is deemed "rare." We're at 11 months. That's if it's a brain mass. The next step, I expect, will be to put him back on Keppra - he went off that a few months ago at the vet's suggestion. The literature suggests that "many dogs regain useful control for months with a two-drug regimen." He had his old pep under the Keppra. If that doesn't work, then they'll suggest a higher dose of the phenobarbital, and/or another drug - which leads to lethargy.
If he can't summon the desire to go to the field or sniff the greenery at Centennial, what's the point?
I know, easy for me to say.
To clarify: I hadn't heard him seize, because we were napping. His sharp bark woke me up, and I was confused - he never does that. Usually rests on his dog bed and waits until I wake. Must be hungry. But he was preternaturally alert, and when I patted his head I felt dampness. Checked his bed: damn. Got him a Frosty Paws for focus, then put everything into the washing machine. He recovered quickly enough, and we went for a walk. Snapped him back into focus, dispelled the disorientation. When we got back I sat on the base of the light pole - again, to clarify, this was the second light pole base, farthest from the Fred; we go there sometimes so my cigar whiff wafts not into the common area. He has big sticks there as well. I'm thinking, I wish the blood work didn't look good, as far as absorption. Maybe it's an
absorption problem.
No, it's a brain tumor problem.
Spent the night doing nothing I can remember, except sorting and clipping and other things I can do with my mind off, or elsewhere. Poured a scotch at 10 and started looking at the websites I will, eventually, need to call.
Jasper was very old and slow, and slept most of the time.
Birch, I am certain, will be alert and engaged, and look at me to be sure it's all okay.
Do I have to take him down the elevator to let the vet in the building, because he'd be unhappy left alone?
Do I have to walk down the hall back to the apartment, watching his ears bounce as he trots back home?
